solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: He's investigating every tape I edited

indicators.note: edited suggests the words have been reworked, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone cuts and edits a recording of every tape they hold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'edited' rearranges the ten letters of EVERY TAPE I.
explanation.definitionFit: A private detective is one who investigates for hire, so 'he's investigating' describes him.

clue.text: Stormy petrel grabbing head of Indian snake?

indicators.note: grabbing means one set of letters holds another inside it
stormy suggests turbulence, so the letters of petrel are tossed about
the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A stormy petrel, a seabird, seizes an Indian snake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stormy' scrambles PETREL to REPTLE, which then grabs I, the first letter of 'Indian'. The question mark flags that a snake is just one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Snakes are one kind of cold-blooded scaly animal, so a snake is an example of the class.

clue.text: Man turning up the telly, guzzling beer

indicators.note: guzzling means swallowing, so one piece takes another inside it
in a down clue turning up reads the letters from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: telly is British slang for television, TV
ale is a type of beer

explanation.surface: A man turns up the TV volume while drinking beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning up' works in a down clue, where the abbreviation reads upwards; 'Man' is the old sense of a gentleman's servant.
explanation.definitionFit: A manservant is often called a man, as in 'my man', a gentleman's personal attendant.

clue.text: See 23
Mrs A. conceitedly revised part of physics syllabus

indicators.note: revised means altered, so the letters are put into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A smug teacher called Mrs A rewrote part of the physics syllabus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revised' rearranges the fifteen letters of MRS A CONCEITEDLY.
explanation.definitionFit: The study of electric currents interacting with magnetic fields is a branch of physics taught in courses.

clue.text: Rising Middle East manager to do relief work

indicators.note: in a down clue rising reads the letters upwards, backwards

parts.note: a boss is a manager

explanation.surface: An up-and-coming Middle Eastern manager volunteers for disaster relief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising' reverses ME to EM. 'Relief work' is not aid but raised decoration.
explanation.definitionFit: Relief is a design raised above a surface, and stamping or carving such a raised pattern is that verb.

clue.text: Scotsman who showed the importance of the transfer of power

definitions.text: Scotsman who showed the importance of the transfer of power

parts.words: Scotsman who showed the importance of the transfer of power
parts.note: The SI unit of power, the rate at which energy is transferred, is named after him

explanation.surface: A Scottish figure demonstrated why handing over power matters, as if in politics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Transfer of power' sounds political, but a power unit measures energy transferred per second, and it bears the Scottish engineer's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish inventor James Watt gave his surname to the SI unit of power, one joule per second.

clue.text: Being inexperienced, reheat mixture to fill "soggy bottoms"

indicators.note: to fill means one piece goes inside another

parts.note: soggy means wet and bottoms are behinds

indicators.note: a mixture of letters is an anagram of them

explanation.surface: A baking-show complaint: reheating a mix to fill pastry with soggy bottoms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixture' scrambles the reheat letters before they go inside. A 'soggy bottom' is a British baking fault, an undercooked pastry base; here bottoms are simply behinds.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone naive and green, like a newborn animal still damp behind its ears.

clue.text: See 7 down
Old mate put on a stone

parts.note: a pal is a mate, a friend

explanation.surface: An old friend gained weight, putting on a stone (14 pounds).
explanation.walkthrough: 'put on a stone' reads as gaining weight; a stone is a British weight of 14 pounds, but here it is a gem.
explanation.definitionFit: This iridescent silica is a gemstone prized in jewellery.

clue.text: Further improved flat racing enthusiast?

parts.note: flat means level or even
a racing fan who wagers on horses is a better, one who bets

explanation.surface: A flat-racing enthusiast, a fan of races without jumps, seems to be improving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat racing' is horse racing without jumps, but 'flat' separates off to mean level.
explanation.definitionFit: Something improved further still is better than before by an additional degree.

clue.text: Little brother taking over first café

indicators.note: taking over means holding another piece within it

parts.note: bro is a shortened, little form of brother
first is written 1ST, read as IST with the 1 as the letter I

explanation.surface: A younger sibling takes charge of the first café.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little' shortens brother to BRO, and the numeral 1 in 1ST is read as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: A small informal restaurant serving simple meals is a kind of café.

clue.text: Setback: sadly erase parts of mosaic

parts.note: the word set taken back, written backwards, gives TES

indicators.note: sadly suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A setback: someone has unhappily rubbed out part of a mosaic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setback' looks like one noun but splits as set, back; 'sadly' is the anagram signal for the second word.
explanation.definitionFit: Mosaics are built from small tiles or cubes of stone or glass, each called a tessera.

clue.text: Romeo's friend Julius drunk, into Brazilian port

parts.note: Julius is the setter, who refers to himself as me

indicators.note: into means one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Rio de Janeiro is a Brazilian port
cut is British slang for drunk

explanation.surface: The setter, drunk, heads into Rio, like a friend of Romeo's.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's own name, Julius, stands for ME. CUT goes inside RIO.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's tragedy, the witty Mercutio is a close companion of Romeo, killed by Tybalt.

clue.text: Lots of bouncers punch Mike touring the States

parts.note: to chin someone is to punch them on the chin

indicators.note: touring means going round, so one piece wraps around another

parts.note: mike and mic are both short for microphone
US is short for the United States

explanation.surface: Nightclub bouncers punch a man named Mike on an American tour.
explanation.walkthrough: The bouncers are not doormen but short-pitched balls aimed at a batsman's head in cricket (or a pitcher's high, tight throw in baseball).
explanation.definitionFit: Chin music is sports slang for a barrage of short-pitched deliveries flying near the batter's face.

clue.text: Poles invested in tech this month

indicators.note: invested in means placed inside, as money is put into something

parts.note: IT, information technology, is tech
N and S are the north and south poles

explanation.surface: Polish investors put money into technology this month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' reads as Polish people but means the magnetic or geographic poles, N and S. The answer is an old letter-writing abbreviation of instant.
explanation.definitionFit: In formal correspondence, the abbreviation for 'instant' means of the current calendar period.

clue.text: Most exciting passion fades away inside

indicators.note: inside means one piece is put within the other

parts.note: heat is passion, as in the heat of the moment
dies means fades away, as a sound dies

explanation.surface: The most thrilling romance has its passion dwindle inwardly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' places the fading word within the passion word, splitting it before its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Heady means intoxicating or thrilling, so the superlative is the most stimulating.

clue.text: Mouth commonly beginning to inflame in desert area

parts.note: gob is a common, slang word for the mouth

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone's mouth starts to flare up in the desert heat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'commonly' signals the vulgar word GOB, British slang for a mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: This vast arid region spanning Mongolia and northern China is a well-known desert.

clue.text: Instrument fitted to Volvo car in America

indicators.note: fitted to means built into, so the answer sits within the words

explanation.surface: A device is installed in a Volvo car sold in America.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer lies across volvO CAR IN America. The surface suggests a dashboard instrument; it is a musical one.
explanation.definitionFit: A small egg-shaped wind flute with finger holes is a musical device for playing tunes.

clue.text: Lie dying, unfortunately giving in

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests something gone awry, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone lies dying, sadly surrendering to death.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfortunately' rearranges LIE DYING.
explanation.definitionFit: Being yielding means surrendering or submitting, which is what giving in describes.

clue.text: Ian upset former pupil visiting Rhode Island capital

indicators.note: in a down clue upset turns the word over, reading it backwards
visiting means going inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: RI is the postal abbreviation for Rhode Island
OB is old boy, a former pupil of a school

explanation.surface: Ian is annoyed that an old schoolmate is visiting Rhode Island's capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' reverses IAN to NAI. OB (old boy) is British for a school's ex-pupil. 'Rhode Island capital' reads as Providence, but 'capital' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This city is the seat of government of Kenya, making it a national capital.

clue.text: Gridiron play doctor introduced to English sister

indicators.note: introduced to means put inside another piece

parts.note: a nun is a religious sister

explanation.surface: A doctor is introduced to an English nurse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sister' suggests a senior nurse in Britain, but here is a religious sister; 'introduced to' puts the doctor inside her, with English placed first.
explanation.definitionFit: In American football, played on a gridiron, a running play around the flank of the defence has this name.

clue.text: Qantas man I approached, crossing part of Australia

indicators.note: crossing means the answer runs across several of these words

explanation.surface: A traveller approached a Qantas airline employee while flying across part of Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs through qanTAS MAN I Approached.
explanation.definitionFit: This island state lies south of the mainland and is one of the six states of the country.

clue.text: Miserable, and soon to be spitting feathers!

definitions.meaning: with down, soft feathers, in your mouth you are about to spit feathers

explanation.surface: Someone miserable is close to spitting feathers, being furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spitting feathers' is a British idiom for being very angry or thirsty; here it is literal, with down (soft feathers) in one's mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes looking or feeling dejected and unhappy, like a mouth turned downward.

clue.text: Product of farmer's wife being in season?

parts.note: a female animal in season is on heat, so heat is that state

explanation.surface: A farmer's wife produces something during the right season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being in season' sounds like ripe produce, but refers to an animal on heat.
explanation.definitionFit: Cereal grain grown for flour is a staple crop produced by arable farms.

clue.text: Cheek! RAF, for example, is something perfunctorily paid

parts.note: lip means cheek, insolent talk
the RAF, Royal Air Force, is one of the armed services

explanation.surface: An outraged cry at the cheek of the Royal Air Force paying something only half-heartedly.
explanation.walkthrough: The RAF is Britain's Royal Air Force, one of its armed services.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means support or respect professed in words without any real action, so it is paid as a token.

clue.text: Lover boy regularly seen in beer house

indicators.note: regularly means every other letter of these words is taken

explanation.surface: A romantic young man is often spotted in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking alternate letters of bEeR hOuSe gives the answer. A 'beer house' is a British pub.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek god of love is a winged boy, the counterpart of Cupid.

clue.text: Spoil Charlie's brandy

parts.note: to mar is to spoil
Charlie is the NATO phonetic alphabet word for C

explanation.surface: Someone ruins Charlie's brandy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie's' reads as possession; the 's is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: This spirit is distilled from the skins and pulp left after pressing grapes, a kind of grape brandy.

clue.text: Like the introduction of Rover cars one after the other?

definitions.meaning: Rover is a typical dog's name, and dogs meeting sniff each other from front to rear
traffic queued closely, each car's front behind the next one's rear

explanation.surface: The launch of a Rover car model, with vehicles arriving in a line.
explanation.walkthrough: Rover is a British car make, but here it is a dog. The phrase also names whole-animal cooking, nothing wasted.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes things lined up front to back, as in a traffic jam, or dogs sniffing each other in greeting.
